newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian pyramid scheme head grabs money and runs.
newsitem.headline: Albanian pyramid scheme head grabs money and runs.

text.p: Albanian officials said on Tuesday the head of a suspected pyramid scheme had disappeared with $13 million, undermining the web of get-rich-quick schemes that had sprung up across the country.
Scores of people from Shkoder, a town 110 km (70 miles) north of Tirana, sued Aleksander Grunasi, head of the Grunasi company, after he fled with the money, a Tirana prosecutor said.
"A lot of people are suing him," the official told Reuters, on condition of anonymity.

Albanian state television, citing an official statement by the prosecutor's office, said authorities had started a penal case against Grunasi, who had offered returns of up to 10 percent a month on money lent to his company.
"Grunasi has left the country together with his family and $13 million," the television reported, citing the statement. It added that eight of the suspect's associates had been arrested.

Pyramid schemes, which can only deliver big returns by sucking in more and more investors, cropped up in Albania after the Balkan nation overthrew communism in 1990, and companies scrambled for cash which the tiny banking system could not supply.

Hundreds of thousands of Albanians, many of them living hand to mouth, were lured by pledges of big returns of sometimes up to 50 percent a month on small investments. Many sold their homes and livestock to join the rush.

"I sold my apartment two years ago and put $10,000 into Grunasi. With interest, the sum has grown into $22,000," said one of Grunasi's depositors, who would only give his name as Ladi. "What can I do now?"

The schemes helped drive up the local currency, the lek, against major currencies and set off alarm bells at the World Bank. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) sent a delegation to Albania, one of the poorest European countries, to scrutinise the business.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Ranjid Teja, head of the IMF mission, said it was not the fund's responsibility to close down such schemes, but warned that the growing number of money schemes could endanger Albania's fragile economic recovery.
"We do feel responsible to point out that these schemes have now grown so much that any problem in this area will create problems not only for the depositors but for the economy as well," he said.

Azem Hajdari, a member of parliament for the ruling Democratic Party and self-declared president of a trade union, called on the IMF to take control of the schemes so that Albanian depositors were guaranteed their savings until a competitive and safe banking system could be created.
Albania's parliament last week decided to set up an independent committee of economic experts to gather information on the pyramid schemes and report their findings to parliament.
